title: Aldehydes, ketones and the carbonyl group
keyIdea: The carbonyl group C=O is polar: oxygen is more electronegative, so carbon is δ+ and oxygen δ−. In an aldehyde the C=O is at the end of the chain (–CHO, name ends -al); in a ketone it is inside the chain (–CO–, name ends -one). The δ+ carbon is where nucleophiles attack.

kid: A carbonyl group is a carbon joined to an oxygen by a double bond, C=O. The two atoms share electrons, but not fairly. Oxygen pulls harder. Its electronegativity is 3.44, and carbon's is 2.55. So the electrons sit nearer the oxygen. Oxygen gets a small negative charge, δ−. Carbon is left with a small positive charge, δ+.

Where the C=O sits sets the family. At the end of a chain, the C=O carbon also holds an H. We write this as CHO. That is an aldehyde, and its name ends in al. Inside the chain, there is a carbon on each side. We write this as CO. That is a ketone, and its name ends in one.

Propanal and propanone both have the formula C3H6O. In propanal the C=O is on carbon 1. In propanone it is on carbon 2. Same atoms, different family. The stem gives the number of carbons: meth is 1, eth is 2, prop is 3, but is 4 and pent is 5.

A ketone needs a carbon on each side, so the smallest one has 3 carbons. Butanone needs no number, since carbon 2 is the only place. In a chain of 5 there are two places, so we write pentan-2-one or pentan-3-one. Count from the end nearest the C=O. Last, the δ+ carbon draws in ions with a lone pair, called nucleophiles.
adult: This topic introduces the carbonyl group, C=O, found in aldehydes and ketones. Learners explain why the bond is polar, tell the two families apart by where the C=O sits, and name simple examples such as propanal, propanone and butanone. It sets up later work on oxidation of alcohols and nucleophilic addition.

In the lab, learners place δ+ and δ− on C=O, then slide the C=O along a 3-carbon chain to see propanal turn into propanone with the same formula. They build molecules from names, sort condensed formulas, and send a cyanide ion to the atom it bonds to, comparing C=O with the non-polar C=C.

Common mistakes: putting δ− on carbon; calling CH3COCH3 an aldehyde because it has the letters CHO in it; writing propan-1-al or ethanone; numbering from the wrong end, as in pentan-4-one; and thinking a negative ion bonds to the oxygen. Another mistake is to read CHO and COH as the same thing; COH is not a carbonyl.
A quick check at home or in class: write a condensed formula and ask the learner to point to the C=O, say which family it is, and name it. Then ask which atom a nucleophile would bond to, and why.

familyTip: Write CH3CH2CHO and CH3COCH3 on two cards. Ask which is the aldehyde and which is the ketone, and how they can share the formula C3H6O.

practice.prompt: In the C=O bond, which atom is δ+ and why?
choices: Oxygen, because it has more electrons
Carbon, because oxygen pulls the shared electrons towards itself
Neither, the bond is shared equally
practice.hint: Compare electronegativity: O is 3.44, C is 2.55.
practice.explain: Oxygen is more electronegative, so it pulls the bonding electrons closer. Oxygen becomes δ− and carbon is left δ+.

practice.prompt: An aldehyde has {n} carbons in a straight chain. Where is its C=O?
choices: On carbon 1, at the end of the chain
practice.explain: In an aldehyde the C=O is always at the end, so it is carbon 1. With {n} carbons, the other carbons follow on from it.

practice.hint: Count the carbons, then decide if C=O is at the end or inside.
practice.explain: There are 4 carbons and the C=O is inside the chain, so it is a ketone: butanone. No number is needed because carbon 2 is the only ketone position.

practice.prompt: A straight-chain aldehyde has {n} carbons. What is its formula?
practice.hint: Aldehydes and ketones share the general formula of one C=O on an alkane chain.
practice.explain: Aldehydes and ketones have the general formula CₙH₂ₙO. With {n} carbons there are twice as many hydrogens and one oxygen.

practice.prompt: Which is the smallest possible ketone?
practice.hint: A ketone needs a carbon on each side of the C=O.
practice.explain: The C=O carbon needs a carbon on each side, so a ketone needs at least 3 carbons. Propanone is the smallest; ethanone does not exist.

pool.prompt: Propanal and propanone are both C₃H₆O. How do they differ?
choices: Propanal has C=O at the end; propanone has it in the middle
pool.hint: Same formula: look at where the C=O sits.
pool.explain: They are isomers. Propanal is an aldehyde with C=O on carbon 1; propanone is a ketone with C=O on carbon 2.

pool.prompt: Which is the correct name for CH₃CH₂CHO?
pool.explain: The C=O of an aldehyde is always carbon 1, so no number is written: propanal.

pool.hint: Number from the end nearest the C=O.
pool.explain: Counting from the left end, the C=O is on carbon 2, so it is pentan-2-one. Counting from the other end gives 4, which is not the lowest number.

pool.prompt: Which condensed formula shows a ketone?
pool.hint: Look for CO with carbon on both sides.
pool.explain: CH₃COCH₂CH₃ has CO between two carbon groups: butanone. CHO is an aldehyde and OH is an alcohol.

pool.prompt: A cyanide ion, CN⁻, attacks a C=O. Which atom does it bond to, and why?
choices: The oxygen, because oxygen is the reactive atom
The carbon, because it is δ+ and attracts the lone pair
pool.hint: A nucleophile looks for positive charge.
pool.explain: CN⁻ is a nucleophile with a lone pair. It is attracted to the δ+ carbon and repelled by the δ− oxygen.

pool.prompt: Why is C=C in an alkene not attacked by nucleophiles like C=O is?
choices: C=C is not polar, so neither carbon is δ+
pool.hint: Compare the two atoms in each bond.
pool.explain: Both atoms in C=C are carbon, so they pull equally and neither is δ+. Alkenes react with electrophiles instead.

pool.prompt: How many hydrogens are in a straight-chain ketone with {n} carbons?
pool.explain: Aldehydes and ketones fit CₙH₂ₙO, so a ketone with {n} carbons has 2 × {n} hydrogens.

pool.prompt: Why does butanone need no position number?
choices: In a 4-carbon chain, carbon 2 is the only place a ketone C=O can go
Numbers are only used for rings
pool.hint: Try putting the C=O on each carbon of a 4-carbon chain.
pool.explain: Carbons 1 and 4 give butanal, and carbons 2 and 3 are the same position counted from each end. So there is only one butanone.

pool.prompt: An aldehyde has {n} carbons. Which group is at the end of its chain?
pool.hint: The C=O carbon in an aldehyde also holds an H.
pool.explain: Every aldehyde, whatever its length, ends in –CHO: the C=O carbon is bonded to one H.

visual.caption: Which family? Drag each name, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: place δ+ and δ− on C=O, turn propanal into propanone, build from names and send a nucleophile to the δ+ carbon.
